region_file: Southeast Asia and Oceania (Malaysia, Thailand, Australia, New Zealand and adjacent)

actors.name: Barisan Revolusi Nasional
actors.description: The dominant insurgent organisation in Thailand's Malay-Muslim deep south, operating across Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat and four districts of Songkhla. Since January 2004 more than 23,000 incidents have been recorded in the conflict, with over 7,700 killed and 14,500 injured. Bank and ATM bombings are a recurring signature: attacks on ATMs of the Islamic Bank of Thailand and the Government Savings Bank have featured in coordinated multi-site waves, chosen as accessible symbols of the Thai state's presence.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The only actor in Southeast Asia that systematically bombs bank infrastructure for political rather than acquisitive reasons. State-linked banks are attacked as symbols of Thai administration, meaning target selection follows ownership rather than cash holdings. Coordinated multi-site waves mean a single event can affect an entire province's ATM availability, and staff safety in the four southern provinces is a standing concern.
ttps: Coordinated multi-site IED and arson waves across several districts in one night
Small explosive devices at ATMs of state-linked banks
Motorcycle-borne and vehicle-borne IEDs
Secondary devices targeting responders
Arson of government-linked commercial premises
Ambushes of security forces and shootings of officials and teachers

existence.basis: Two decades of documented insurgency; Deep South Watch and Human Rights Watch reporting.

attribution.basis: BRN is assessed to conduct the majority of attacks but rarely claims them, which is a deliberate feature of its operating model.

financial_targeting.basis: Bank ATMs and branches are a documented recurring target category.

notable_incidents.summary: Wave of arson and bombings; blasts damaged an ATM of the Islamic Bank of Thailand and an ATM of the Government Savings Bank among multiple simultaneous attacks.
Human Rights Watch reported new insurgent attacks on civilians despite a public BRN pledge not to target them; 57 attacks in April alone caused 18 deaths and 50 injuries.

watch_indicators: Anniversary dates and negotiation breakdowns preceding attack waves
Multi-site simultaneous incidents indicating a coordinated campaign night
Attacks on state-linked commercial premises as a precursor to bank targeting

actors.name: Mekong scam compound operators
actors.description: Chinese-led criminal syndicates operating industrial-scale fraud compounds in territory controlled by armed groups along the Myanmar-Thailand border and in Cambodia and Laos. KK Park and Shwe Kokko are purpose-built cities dedicated to online fraud, sited in territory held by the Karen Border Guard Force and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army. Workers are frequently trafficked and held under armed guard, which makes this simultaneously a fraud, human trafficking and armed-group financing problem. Demolition campaigns in 2025 proved largely cosmetic: KK Park infrastructure was demolished while Shwe Kokko buildings were merely sealed, and operations resumed within two months.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The single largest source of scam-driven financial crime affecting Malaysian, Thai, Australian and Western retail banking. UNODC estimates just under USD 40 billion in annual revenue for the syndicates. The physical dimension matters for banks because it explains the mule account and cash-out infrastructure: compounds require recruiters, mule handlers, cash couriers and crypto OTC desks in Malaysia, Thailand and beyond, and those are physical networks operating inside bank customer bases.
ttps: Industrial-scale romance, investment and task-based fraud run from guarded compounds
Human trafficking and debt bondage of compound workers
Payment of protection to armed groups controlling the territory
Layered laundering through mule accounts, OTC desks, USDT and gold
Rapid relocation and reconstitution after enforcement action
Recruitment of mule account holders and cash couriers in target-country banking systems

existence.basis: UNODC reporting, US Scam Center Strike Force, extensive investigative journalism and enforcement action.

attribution.basis: Operating syndicates and host armed groups are identified; individual compound ownership is often opaque and contested.

financial_targeting.basis: Retail banking customers worldwide are the victim base and banking rails are the laundering channel.

notable_incidents.summary: Junta and allied Border Guard Force conducted a publicised crackdown a week after the US announced its Scam Center Strike Force; KK Park infrastructure was demolished while Shwe Kokko buildings were only sealed. Operations resumed within two months.
Scam victims in the region were defrauded of up to USD 37 billion; UNODC estimates just under USD 40 billion annual revenue for the syndicates.

actors.name: Karen Border Guard Force and Democratic Karen Benevolent Army
actors.description: Armed ethnic militia formations controlling the Myawaddy border area where the largest scam compounds are sited. They provide land, security, utilities and protection to the syndicates in exchange for rent and a share of proceeds, which makes them the physical guarantors of the region's fraud economy. Their participation in publicised crackdowns has been assessed by observers as pressure relief rather than genuine disruption.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: These are the actors that make scam compounds physically defensible. Any assessment of whether Southeast Asian fraud volumes will fall has to model militia incentives rather than compound raids. Sanctions exposure is the direct banking consequence, since designated militia leaders and their business networks reach into Thai and regional commerce.
ttps: Provision of land, power, telecoms and armed protection to fraud syndicates
Rent extraction and revenue sharing from compound operators
Border control and taxation of movement and goods
Participation in performative enforcement to relieve international pressure
Shielding of compound assets and personnel from Myanmar and Thai authorities

existence.basis: Well-documented militia formations with named leadership; subject to UK and US sanctions.

attribution.basis: Territorial control and compound siting are established by multiple independent investigations.

financial_targeting.basis: Relevance is as enabler and sanctions-exposed counterparty rather than direct attacker.

notable_incidents.summary: BGF participated with the junta in a publicised crackdown; independent reporting assessed the demolitions as selective and the sealing of Shwe Kokko as reversible.

watch_indicators: New sanctions listings of militia leadership and linked companies
Thai-side business relationships with designated individuals

actors.name: Regional illicit financial service conglomerates
actors.description: Cambodia-headquartered conglomerates providing the financial and marketplace infrastructure that scam compounds depend on, including guarantee escrow services, payment processing, currency exchange and, in some cases, licensed banking. Their significance is that they blur the boundary between the illicit compound economy and licensed regional finance, holding banking licences and correspondent relationships while servicing fraud proceeds.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The clearest correspondent banking risk in Southeast Asia, because these entities have at times held genuine licences and legitimate-looking relationships. Malaysian, Thai, Singaporean and Australian institutions with regional correspondent exposure need to track designations and ownership chains here, not just the compounds themselves.

Payment processing and currency exchange for compound proceeds
Use of licensed banking and payment entities to obtain correspondent access

attribution.basis: Corporate structures are deliberately opaque; beneficial ownership is contested in places.

financial_targeting.basis: Regulated financial infrastructure is the operating medium.

watch_indicators: New designations naming regional conglomerates or their subsidiaries

actors.name: Thai mule account recruitment and cash-out networks
actors.description: Networks that recruit Thai nationals to open bank accounts and rent them to fraud syndicates, plus the cash-out layer of couriers, OTC brokers and gold dealers that converts proceeds. The scale is exceptional: Thai banks froze approximately three million accounts in a 2025 crackdown, and authorities closed over 351,000 mule accounts and froze assets worth more than 3.6 billion baht in a nine-month period. The crackdown also ensnared thousands of legitimate account holders, which is itself a lesson about blunt controls.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: This is where Southeast Asian fraud proceeds physically enter and leave the Thai banking system, and it is the layer Thai institutions are directly accountable for. Recruitment is conducted in person and online, and increasingly involves coercion; some mule holders are victims. Distinguishing coerced or duped mules from willing ones is now a live compliance and consumer-duty problem.
ttps: Recruitment of account holders through social media, workplace and community networks
Purchase or rental of accounts, often from economically vulnerable individuals
Layered movement of funds through many accounts before conversion
Conversion to USDT through OTC desks, then mixers or cross-chain swaps
Settlement through gold bullion purchase and informal currency exchange
Cross-border courier movement of cash and gold to Myanmar and Cambodia

actors.name: Thai gold shop robbery and gold-laundering cluster
actors.description: Two overlapping phenomena around Thai gold shops. First, armed robbery of gold retailers, an established Thai crime pattern that occasionally produces mass-casualty incidents. Second, and more significant for banks, the use of gold purchase as a laundering step for scam proceeds, which prompted the Bank of Thailand to require gold shops to report all transactions and to increase scrutiny of crypto-settled gold purchases.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Gold is Thailand's principal non-bank store of value and its principal laundering off-ramp. The 2026 reporting requirements make gold shops a de facto reporting entity, and institutions financing or banking gold retailers inherit that exposure. The robbery dimension matters for banks that provide cash services and lending to gold retailers.
ttps: Armed robbery of gold retailers in shopping centres and provincial towns
Purchase of gold with fraud proceeds to convert digital value into a portable asset
Crypto-settled gold purchase to break the transaction trail
Onward export or resale of bullion to complete integration

existence.basis: Thai regulatory action and sustained crime reporting.

attribution.basis: Robbery crews are individual; laundering use is systemic rather than attributable to one network.

financial_targeting.basis: Gold retail sits adjacent to banking; the laundering channel is the primary institutional exposure.

notable_incidents.summary: Bank of Thailand tightened controls on gold and FX markets, requiring gold shops to report all transactions and increasing scrutiny of crypto-settled payments.

watch_indicators: Gold retailer customers with turnover inconsistent with footfall
Crypto-settled purchases at financed gold retailers

actors.name: Malaysian Ah Long illegal moneylending syndicates
actors.description: Unlicensed moneylending syndicates operating nationwide in Malaysia, enforcing repayment through harassment, vandalism and intimidation. Signature tactics include splashing red paint on borrowers' homes, vehicles and workplaces, posting threatening notices, and calling at night. The MCA's public complaints bureau recorded 165 moneylending cases involving RM18.6 million by mid-2025, with over 85 percent from the Chinese community. Enforcers have shifted from firebombing toward psychological intimidation, precisely because arson attracts heavier charges.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The dominant informal credit competitor in Malaysia and a direct driver of customer financial distress, coerced withdrawals and account misuse. Borrowers are frequently required to hand over ATM cards and online banking credentials as collateral, which converts a loan sharking problem into an account takeover and mule account problem inside the bank. Branches and their staff are occasionally targeted when a borrower is traced to a workplace.
ttps: Red paint splashing on homes, vehicles and business premises
Threatening notices and staged imagery sent by messaging apps
Night-time harassment calls and visits to family and employers
Retention of borrower ATM cards, bank credentials and identity documents
Historic use of firebombing, now reduced due to heavier sentencing
Recruitment of borrowers into mule account provision to clear debt

existence.basis: Malaysian prosecutions and MCA public complaints data.

attribution.basis: Highly fragmented syndicates; enforcers are prosecuted, principals rarely.

financial_targeting.basis: Bank customers and their credentials are directly exploited; institutions are not attacked.

notable_incidents.summary: Two men linked to an illegal moneylending syndicate pleaded guilty to vandalism charges including splashing paint on homes and vehicles, alongside harassment and drug offences.
MCA reported 165 moneylending-related cases involving RM18.6 million, and noted a shift from paint and firebombs toward psychological intimidation such as staged wake photographs.

actors.name: Malaysian mule account and syndicate recruitment networks
actors.description: Networks recruiting Malaysians to open and surrender bank accounts, e-wallets and SIM cards to fraud syndicates, including those operating from Mekong compounds. Recruitment happens through social media, campus networks, employment scams and loan shark debt clearance. Bank Negara Malaysia and PDRM have run repeated National Scam Response Centre and account-freezing campaigns.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The point at which Southeast Asian fraud proceeds enter Malaysian banking. It is also where the coercion picture matters: a meaningful share of mule holders are debt-coerced by loan sharks or trafficked, and treating all of them as offenders creates consumer-protection risk. Institutions face account-opening abuse, rapid pass-through and freezing-order operational load.
ttps: Recruitment via social media job advertisements and campus networks
Purchase or rental of accounts, e-wallets and registered SIM cards
Debt-clearance arrangements with loan sharks in exchange for account provision
High-velocity layering through many accounts before withdrawal or crypto conversion
Cash courier movement to regional syndicate hubs

existence.basis: Bank Negara Malaysia and PDRM enforcement, sustained national reporting.

attribution.basis: Recruiters prosecuted individually; syndicate control is offshore.

financial_targeting.basis: Bank accounts are the traded commodity.

watch_indicators: New accounts with immediate high-velocity inbound and outbound flow

actors.name: Malaysian secret societies and numbered gangs
actors.description: Malaysia's long-established numbered secret societies, drawing on both Chinese triad and Indian gang traditions, proscribed under national security legislation. Their core economies are extortion of businesses, illegal gambling, debt collection, drug distribution and control of informal moneylending. They provide the enforcement layer for much of the Ah Long economy.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The enforcement infrastructure behind illegal moneylending and unlicensed debt collection, and a source of extortion pressure on SME banking customers. They also supply the personnel who recover ATM cards and credentials from indebted borrowers, which is where they intersect most directly with bank fraud losses.
ttps: Extortion and protection collection from businesses and entertainment venues
Violent debt collection on behalf of illegal moneylenders
Control of illegal gambling and its cash flows
Recruitment of youths for enforcement tasks
Laundering through cash-intensive businesses

existence.basis: Malaysian proscription lists and sustained police action.

attribution.basis: Gang identities are formally recognised; individual incident attribution varies.

financial_targeting.basis: Bank customers are affected; institutions are not directly attacked.

watch_indicators: SME customers in entertainment and hospitality reporting protection demands

actors.name: Malaysian money changer and remittance robbery cluster
actors.description: Armed and edged-weapon robbery of money changers, remittance agents and their couriers in Malaysia, frequently involving insider information about currency supply runs and, in at least one documented case, serving police officers as the perpetrators. Losses in individual incidents have ranged from RM120,000 to RM8 million.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Money services businesses are the softest cash-holding financial nodes in Malaysia, with less protective infrastructure than bank branches but comparable cash volumes at peak times. Insider involvement, including impersonation of police, is a consistent feature and is the control failure most worth addressing.
ttps: Armed or machete robbery of money changer outlets during trading hours
Interception of currency supply runs between outlets
Impersonation of police officers to gain compliance
Insider tipping on cash and currency holdings
Targeting of outlets in shopping complexes with multiple exits

attribution.basis: Crews are individual; some cases involve corrupt officials.

financial_targeting.basis: Money services businesses and their cash movements are the sole target.

actors.name: Malaysian snatch theft and device-theft cluster
actors.description: Motorcycle-borne snatch theft of bags and phones, historically a signature Malaysian street crime associated with Mat Rempit riding culture. Its financial significance has changed: where the value was once the physical contents, it is now the banking and e-wallet apps on the stolen handset, mirroring the London pattern.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Malaysia has very high mobile banking and e-wallet penetration, so a snatched unlocked handset gives immediate access to accounts, wallets and DuitNow transfers. The same authentication assumption that fails in London, that possession of the enrolled device implies the legitimate customer, fails here, with the added factor that many victims cannot immediately report from the stolen device.
ttps: Motorcycle pillion snatch of bags and handsets from pedestrians and vehicle windows
Targeting near ATMs, markets and transport hubs
Immediate exploitation of unlocked banking and e-wallet apps
Resale of handsets through informal markets
Occasional escalation to assault when the victim resists

existence.basis: Long-running Malaysian crime statistics and reporting.

attribution.basis: Opportunistic and dispersed offending.

financial_targeting.basis: Device contents rather than the device drive the modern financial loss, though the theft itself is opportunistic.

watch_indicators: Wallet transfers immediately following a reported device loss

actors.name: West African fraud syndicates in Malaysia
actors.description: Nigerian and other West African syndicates operating from Malaysia, typically using student visas as cover, running romance and business email compromise fraud with local recruitment of Malaysian mules and, frequently, local partners who open accounts. Malaysian police conduct regular enforcement operations against them.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: A persistent source of romance and BEC fraud losses booked against Malaysian and international accounts, with a distinctive local recruitment pattern: Malaysian women recruited as romantic partners then used to open and operate accounts. This makes the mule holder simultaneously a fraud victim and an account offender, which complicates both freezing decisions and remediation.

actors.name: Comanchero and Australian outlaw motorcycle gangs
actors.description: Australia's outlaw motorcycle gangs, of which the Comancheros are currently the most transnationally capable, function as franchised organised crime networks rather than as clubs. They control significant shares of the illicit tobacco, drug distribution and extortion markets, and have been central to the Melbourne tobacco war arson campaign. Leadership frequently operates offshore from Dubai, Turkey and Thailand.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Two exposures. Extortion and arson against small businesses, which shows up as SME customer distress, insurance claims and coerced payment patterns. And laundering, where OMCG-linked networks use cash-intensive businesses, cryptocurrency and professional facilitators; AUSTRAC has repeatedly flagged the sector. There is also a documented history of attempts to recruit insiders in banking and telecommunications.

Arson and firebombing of non-compliant retail premises
Drive-by shootings and demonstrative violence
Laundering through cash-intensive businesses, crypto and professional facilitators
Offshore leadership directing domestic operations via encrypted platforms
Recruitment of insiders in banking, telecoms and logistics

actors.name: Melbourne tobacco war arson-for-hire cluster
actors.description: A sustained arson and extortion campaign in Melbourne, running from March 2023, in which rival networks firebomb tobacconists, vape shops and associated businesses to enforce control of the illicit tobacco market. Victoria Police established Taskforce Lunar in response; by early 2026 the running tally had cleared 200 arson attacks with more than 100 arrests. The executors are typically young, recruited for individual jobs and paid small sums, which mirrors the Nordic violence-as-a-service model.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The most consequential Australian pattern of physical attacks on commercial premises, and therefore on bank SME customers, their collateral and their insurance. It also produces a recognisable extortion signature in SME account behaviour. Because the executors are recruited disposably, the pattern generalises: any Australian business, including financial service points, can be firebombed cheaply on a third party's instruction.

Recruitment of young executors for small payments via encrypted apps
Extortion demands preceding or following the attack

attribution.basis: Executors charged; commissioning networks partly identified.

financial_targeting.basis: Financial institutions are not targeted; exposure is through SME customers and the demonstrated availability of cheap arson.

actors.description: Family- and area-based Sydney networks engaged in drug distribution, extortion and a long-running series of public shootings against rivals. actors.name: Long River money laundering organisation
actors.description: A Chinese organised crime group that operated the Changjiang Currency Exchange, a shopfront remittance business with a national Australian footprint, as a laundering vehicle. The AFP alleged it laundered almost AUD 229 million in three years while transferring more than AUD 10 billion in total, including proceeds of cybercrime against victims. Operation Avarus-Nightwolf, a 14-month AFP-led investigation supported by AUSTRAC, ABF, ACIC, ASIC, ATO and US HSI, produced seven charges and over AUD 50 million restrained.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The most instructive Australian case of a licensed-looking remittance business operating as a criminal laundering utility, with modern retail shopfronts specifically designed to project legitimacy. For banks it is a direct lesson in MSB counterparty risk: the business held banking relationships and looked entirely conventional from the outside.

Commingling of legitimate remittance flows with criminal proceeds

actors.name: Australian and New Zealand ram-raid and ATM removal crews
actors.description: Crews, predominantly juvenile, that drive stolen vehicles into retail premises to seize cash drawers, ATMs, safes and high-value stock. New Zealand recorded a 400 percent increase in ram raids between 2017 and 2022, with 76 percent of those arrested under 18 and 14 percent connected to organised crime, prompting dedicated legislation. Australian incidence follows a similar youth-led pattern with adult organised crime involvement at the fencing layer.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The main destructive threat to in-store ATMs and retail cash holdings in both countries. The organised crime linkage is at the disposal end rather than the offence end, which means enforcement against individual juveniles does not reduce demand. For deployers the practical implication is siting and anchoring in convenience retail rather than perimeter security.
ttps: Stolen vehicles driven through shopfronts in the early hours
Removal of ATMs, safes and cash drawers within a short dwell time
Social media coordination and 'post and boast' publication
Fencing of proceeds through adult organised crime networks
Repeat targeting of premises with weak bollarding

attribution.basis: Predominantly juvenile ad hoc groups.

financial_targeting.basis: ATMs and cash are among several targets alongside retail stock.

actors.name: Virtual kidnapping and coercion cluster targeting Chinese-speaking communities
actors.description: Syndicates that contact Chinese international students and recent migrants posing as Chinese police or embassy officials, convince them they are implicated in a crime, then coerce them into staging their own kidnapping, photographing themselves bound, and cutting contact while a ransom is extracted from family in China. Australian and New Zealand police have run repeated public awareness campaigns because the missing-person response consumes substantial resource.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: Produces coerced large transfers, account emptying and family-funded remittances that look like legitimate student support payments. Victims are actively coached to deceive bank staff, and the manufactured urgency defeats normal cooling-off interventions. It also generates duress situations inside branches that staff are rarely trained to recognise.

Manufactured criminal accusation with threat of deportation or prosecution
Coercion of the victim to self-isolate and stage abduction imagery
Ransom extraction from family overseas while the victim is unreachable
Coaching of the victim to mislead banks and universities about transfers

actors.name: Australian card skimming and mail-theft cluster
actors.description: Crews that combine ATM and POS skimming with theft of mail from unsecured letterboxes and apartment mailrooms to intercept newly issued cards, PIN mailers and identity documents. Australia's high proportion of apartment living and communal mailrooms sustains the mail-theft component, which also feeds identity takeover and fraudulent account opening.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The main physical channel for Australian card and identity compromise. It targets the card issuance process itself, which is a control most institutions treat as a logistics matter rather than a security one. It also intersects with account opening fraud, since intercepted documents support synthetic and stolen identity applications.
ttps: Overlay skimmers and pinhole cameras at ATMs and unattended terminals
Theft of mail from communal letterboxes and apartment mailrooms
Interception of newly issued cards and PIN mailers
Use of stolen identity documents for fraudulent account opening
Rapid cash-out before the legitimate customer notices non-delivery

existence.basis: Australian state police reporting and prosecutions.

attribution.basis: Small crews with no persistent identity.

financial_targeting.basis: Cards, PINs and identity documents are the target.

watch_indicators: Card non-delivery reports clustered by postcode or building
First use of a newly issued card in an unexpected geography
Common-point-of-purchase clustering on a single terminal

actors.name: Australian aggravated home invasion and follow-home robbery crews
actors.description: Crews, frequently youth-dominated, conducting aggravated burglaries and home invasions targeting luxury vehicles, watches, jewellery and, increasingly, cryptocurrency access. Victoria and Queensland have seen sustained increases with significant political salience. A subset targets business owners known to hold cash at home, and a further subset targets known crypto holders.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The Australian expression of the global shift toward attacking wealth at the residence rather than the institution. Private banking and business banking customers are the exposed population, and the crypto-targeting subset connects directly to the wrench attack pattern seen in France and North America.
ttps: Forced entry to occupied homes at night to obtain vehicle keys and valuables
Targeting of luxury vehicles for immediate theft and export or rebirthing
Selection of business owners assessed to hold cash at home
Coercion of cryptocurrency transfers in a growing subset of cases
Social media identification of affluent targets

existence.basis: Victorian and Queensland police statistics and prosecutions.

attribution.basis: Ad hoc youth crews with fluid composition.

financial_targeting.basis: Wealthy individuals including bank customers are targeted; crypto coercion is an emerging subset.

watch_indicators: Client reports of surveillance or attempted entry at residences
Public disclosure of client wealth or crypto holdings
Home invasion clusters in affluent suburbs with client concentration

actors.name: Macau scam call-centre syndicates
actors.description: Chinese-language telecom fraud syndicates, historically Taiwanese-led, that impersonate police, prosecutors and bank officials to convince victims their accounts are implicated in crime and to transfer funds to 'safe' accounts. Call centres are established in rented premises across Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia and the Philippines, and are periodically raided with large numbers of operators detained and deported.
actors.financial_sector_relevance: The dominant impersonation fraud typology affecting Chinese-speaking customers in Malaysia and across the region. It specifically weaponises the bank's own identity and authority, coaches victims to lie to branch staff, and produces coerced transfers that pass normal authentication. The physical dimension is the call-centre premises themselves and the mule and courier layer that follows.
ttps: Impersonation of police, prosecutors and bank anti-fraud teams
Multi-stage scripts escalating from a parcel or account notification to a criminal accusation
Instruction to transfer funds to a 'safe account' under investigation
Coaching of victims to conceal the purpose from bank staff
Operation from rented premises across multiple Southeast Asian jurisdictions
Cash-out through mule accounts and cross-border couriers

existence.basis: Repeated multi-country raids and mass deportations; sustained regional reporting.

attribution.basis: Operators detained; controlling syndicates rarely identified.

financial_targeting.basis: Bank identity and bank transfers are integral to the method.

watch_indicators: Customers making urgent transfers to newly added domestic beneficiaries
Customers on live calls during branch or app transactions
Beneficiary accounts receiving from multiple unrelated victims
